claims.text: In situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy with a dedicated heating stage can reveal atomic-scale structural changes in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles during thermal activation.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
Au, Co, Cu, Ni, and Pt are uniformly distributed in the nanoparticles at room temperature.
The nanoparticles will be heated progressively in a TEM heating holder under controlled conditions.
A controlled temperature ramp and isothermal holds can be used to monitor atomic rearrangements at different thermal steps.
Relevant structural responses include changes in lattice configuration, defects, grain boundaries, and the initiation of elemental segregation.
Thermal activation induces atomic diffusion and rearrangement by overcoming local energy barriers.
Thermodynamic contributions may enhance the resistance of these nanoparticles to significant atomic-scale reorganization up to a temperature threshold.
The nanoparticles will maintain a nearly equiatomic, disordered structure with minimal phase separation below a specific temperature threshold.
The thermal-stability threshold is likely to lie in the mid-hundreds of degrees Celsius.
Above the threshold, subtle atomic rearrangements or the onset of elemental segregation may occur.
The room-temperature baseline has a homogeneous atomic distribution.
Thermal stability may depend on nanoparticle size and temperature range.
The resolution of in situ TEM may limit detection of very small-scale structural changes.
Temperature thresholds and atomic-diffusion kinetics may vary with synthesis conditions and nanoparticle size distribution.
Electron diffraction patterns can assess crystallographic changes during heating.
EDS mapping may permit tracking of elemental redistribution during heating.
